title: Thekua Goes Global: PM Modi Gifts Bihar's Ancient Chhath Cookie to Slovak Speaker
excerpt: Prime Minister Narendra Modi presented thekua, a traditional Bihari sweet snack tied to Chhath Puja, to Slovakia's Speaker Richard Raši during his Europe visit — sparking pride and export dreams among Bihar's thekua makers.
body:
• PM Modi gifted thekua, a traditional Bihari sweet snack, to Slovak Parliament Speaker Richard Raši during his state visit to Slovakia in June 2026
  • Thekua is a deep-fried cookie made from wheat flour, jaggery, ghee, and fennel seeds — closely associated with Chhath Puja and sun worship traditions dating back to Vedic times
  • Bihar's thekua makers are celebrating the gesture as a branding opportunity, with some comparing it to how PM Modi's earlier gifting of jhalmuri boosted demand for the Bengali snack
  • The gift was part of a curated selection that also included a GI-tagged Himru silk tie, a brass Dokra antelope set, and a copy of the Charaka Samhita

When Prime Minister Narendra Modi sat down with Slovak Parliament Speaker Richard Raši during his two-nation European tour in June, the diplomatic gifts included something unexpected: thekua, a dense, golden cookie from Bihar that has been baked for centuries as an offering to the sun god.

The gesture turned a regional festival snack into front-page news in Bihar and sent a ripple of excitement through the state's community of thekua makers.

What Is Thekua?

Thekua — sometimes called a "desi cookie" — is a deep-fried sweet snack native to Bihar and Jharkhand. The classic recipe calls for wheat flour, jaggery or sugar, ghee, and fennel seeds, though some cooks add desiccated coconut and cardamom. The dough is pressed into decorative wooden molds, then fried until crisp on the outside and dense-yet-soft within.

The snack is inseparable from Chhath Puja, the ancient festival of sun worship observed primarily in Bihar, Jharkhand, and eastern Uttar Pradesh. During Chhath, families spend hours preparing thekua as a sacred offering. It is then distributed among relatives, neighbors, and devotees.

Food historians trace thekua's roots to "Apoop," a sweet preparation mentioned in Vedic literature. The core recipe — wheat, jaggery, milk, ghee — has remained largely unchanged over millennia, though the decorative molds and shapes have evolved.

Why It Lasts for Weeks

One of thekua's most practical qualities is its durability. Made with pure ghee and deep-fried to drive out moisture, the cookie stays fresh for extended periods without refrigeration — weeks in many cases. This made it an ideal food for travel and trade in pre-modern Bihar, and it is what makes it a fitting diplomatic gift: it can survive the journey from India to Bratislava without a cold chain.

Bihar's Reaction

The response in Bihar was immediate and enthusiastic. Thekua sellers and makers spoke to media about brightened business prospects.

"This is a very big achievement. Our Bihar's thekua was served there. As people abroad recognise it, the demand for our product will rise immensely."

— Anil Kumar Thakur, thekua seller

Another maker, Shankar Shah, drew an ambitious parallel: "Just like Britannia sells biscuits, we will also sell thekua." Digha MLA Dr. Sanjeev Chaurasia said the gift carried "the message of Chhath's faith and India's cultural heritage to a global audience."

The optimism echoes what happened when PM Modi gifted jhalmuri, a Bengali puffed rice snack, during a stopover in West Bengal — the gesture boosted demand and visibility for the street food.

The Diplomatic Gift Basket

Thekua was part of a carefully curated gift selection that showcased India's regional diversity. Modi also presented Raši with a brass Dokra antelope set, a GI-tagged Himru silk tie and pocket square, a Kotheva art piece from Rajasthan, and a copy of the Charaka Samhita — an ancient Ayurvedic medical text attributed to Acharya Charaka.

During the same visit, Modi met Slovak PM Robert Fico for a high-tea interaction, announced a labour migration MoU to boost professional mobility between India and Slovakia, and invited Fico to visit India.

How to Make Thekua at Home

For diaspora families missing the taste of Chhath, thekua is straightforward to make: mix 2 cups wheat flour with 1 cup powdered jaggery, 3 tablespoons ghee, a teaspoon of fennel seeds, and enough water to form a stiff dough. Shape into small discs or press into molds, and deep-fry on medium heat until golden brown. Store in an airtight container — they will keep for two to three weeks.
